entries.title: The Mughal Empire
entries.summary: The Mughal Empire was a major Islamic empire in the Indian subcontinent, founded by Babur in 1526, known for administrative synthesis, monumental architecture, and cultural flourishing.
entries.detailed_information: Babur, a Timurid prince, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526). Under Akbar, the empire expanded and developed flexible governance. Jahangir and Shah Jahan continued imperial consolidation; Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal. Aurangzeb expanded furthest south but faced sustained resistance and fiscal strain. After the 18th century, Mughal power declined under regional states and colonial pressure; 1857 marks a conventional end associated with the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II.
entries.historical_significance: One of the great early modern Islamic empires; profound impact on South Asian culture and history.
related_questions: What is the Taj Mahal's historical context?
How did the Mughal Empire begin?
entries.source: Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama; John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire

entries.title: Babur and Akbar
entries.summary: Babur founded Mughal rule in India (1526). Akbar later transformed the empire through expansion, administrative systems, and policies of broader incorporation.
entries.detailed_information: Babur's memoirs (Baburnama) provide a rare royal autobiography. After Humayun's interrupted reign, Akbar built a durable imperial structure: mansabdari military-administrative ranking, revenue systems, and a court culture engaging multiple communities. Historical evaluations of Akbar's religious experiments (e.g., Din-i Ilahi) differ and should be handled carefully.
entries.location: North India and expanding Mughal domains
entries.historical_significance: Foundation and consolidation of Mughal imperial order.
entries.disputed_notes: Interpretations of Akbar's religious policies vary among historians.
entries.source: Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama; John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire
